extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and personal essays (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A first-person moral/philosophical essay reflecting on human conduct (here: repentance, private vs public duty), mixing anecdote, classical citation, and personal observation to argue standards of virtue. Geared to readers of reflective, literary moral prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public utility does not automatically justify private immorality
rubrics_metrics.description: The public may sometimes justify actions that violate private morality, but such examples are 'dangerous', 'rare and sickly exceptions' and must be treated with 'great moderation and circumspection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extreme caution before excusing personal breaches of morality for public benefit; only manifest and very great public concern can warrant it. Example: Timoleon's fratricide was excused only because his subsequent conduct and fortune justified it; the Senate deferred judgment given the danger of setting precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging high-stakes acts when personally implicated; prefer impartial adjudicators
rubrics_metrics.description: When a fact presents two important and contrary aspects, those most concerned should refrain from positively determining it and refer it to others 'who were not so much concerned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional or communal decisions should sometimes delegate judgment to less-interested parties to avoid biased or dangerous precedents (illustrated by Syracusans referring Timoleon's conduct to Corinthians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths made under coercion remain binding when fear is removed
rubrics_metrics.description: 'What fear has once made me willing to do, I am obliged to do it when I am no longer in fear; and though that fear only prevailed with my tongue without forcing my will, yet am I bound to keep my word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues against the notion that being coerced (e.g., by robbers) absolves one from promises; a promise induced by fear still obliges the individual unless the promise itself was unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only illicit promises may be lawfully broken
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only lawful, on account of private interest, to excuse breach of promise when the promise was 'unlawful and wicked in itself'; otherwise right of virtue supersedes obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use private gain as excuse to break lawful promises; moral right takes precedence unless the promise itself commanded something immoral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of courage should not require contempt for friendship and private obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: True courage (e.g., Epaminondas) can combine ferocity in war with tenderness and humanity; greatness does not demand abandoning friendship, private duties, or one's word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admire public bravery tempered by private goodness; reject exhortations that glorify betrayal or treachery in service to public causes (quotes from Livy, Ovid, and Lucan reinforce limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not harden conscience in service of public glory; prefer humane imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject 'wicked, bloody, and treacherous natures' that pretend public reasons; set aside extravagant justice and 'stick to more human imitations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public or military demands should not be an automatic license to commit treachery or cruelty; cultural and classical exemplars demonstrate restraint and humanity even in war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private life is the truest test of virtue; public deeds are insufficient evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is better shown by orderliness in private life and ordinary actions than by spectacular public exploits: 'The virtue of the soul does not consist in flying high, but in walking orderly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a person's moral state by how they behave at home, in small duties and ordinary interactions, not merely by grand public acts. Retirement and private duties may be as or more difficult than public offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely primarily on your own conscience to judge yourself, not public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: One should 'have my laws and my judicature to judge of myself' and 'stick to your own' rather than ground virtue upon the approbation of others, which is uncertain and unsafe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal standards of judgment; public praise or blame are unreliable guides, and seeking others' approval is a poor foundation for virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: True repentance requires a complete change of will, not mere wish or dissatisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is 'a recanting of the will' and must 'sting me all over'—superficial, half-way, or ceremonious remorse is not true repentance; mere desire to be other than one is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between wishing one were better and actual moral reformation; real repentance must deeply and universally alter one's dispositions and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual, deliberate sins resist sudden repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sins that are long-rooted, deliberate, and repeatedly contrived 'are not subject to contradiction' and are unlikely to be genuinely and suddenly repented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claimed sudden conversions from long-practiced vice; genuine cure requires more than momentary resolution—it requires transformation of settled will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeit devotion is easy without life-change
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotion's essence is 'abstruse and occult; the appearance easy and ostentatious'—men can counterfeit piety if they do not conform manners and life to profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test professions of piety by observable changes in behavior and life, not by appearances or ostentatious displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate impulsive sins from those of temperament or vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sins are 'impetuous, prompt, and sudden' and distinct from habitual sins of complexion or profession that are deliberated and contrived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat impulsive lapses differently from settled vices when assessing repentance or responsibility; the latter require deeper remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ground virtue's reward on public approbation; the vulgar's opinion is injurious
rubrics_metrics.description: To ground the recompense of virtuous actions upon the approbation of others is 'too uncertain and unsafe,' especially in a corrupt age where 'what before had been vices are now manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek inward satisfaction of conscience rather than popularity; public esteem can be misleading or perverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education may cover but not root out original inclinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural inclinations are 'not to be rooted out; they may be covered and concealed'—education assists and fortifies but seldom alters fundamental constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that deep-seated temperaments persist despite training; reformation often masks rather than eradicates original propensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: External reforms of manners risk neglecting essential vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who attempt to correct the manners of the world by new opinions may reform seeming vices while leaving 'essential vices' as they were, perhaps even augmenting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware reforms that focus on showy, cheap changes; true moral improvement must address interior causes, not only outward manners (Montaigne warns of 'expiat[ing] good cheap').

rubrics_metrics.name: When giving advice, act candidly but accept limited responsibility for outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne gives candid advice 'without sticking' and is 'very indifferent' to reproach if the result goes against his counsel; the fault lies with those who consulted him if they do not profit by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer frank counsel based on judgment, but recognize you cannot guarantee others' use of that counsel; do not overburden yourself with responsibility for clients' or friends' choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake bodily debility or decline for moral repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Old age's abstinence or weakness ('a profound satiety', 'drowsy and rheumatic virtue') should not be conflated with true conscience or repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral reformation by volitional change, not merely by diminished appetites or physical incapacity that limit behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence and judgment are limited by unforeseeable contingencies; misfortune is not always culpable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some errors arise 'not for want of good understanding, but for want of good luck' due to 'secret, and not to be foreseen, parts in matters'—if prudence could not foresee them, blame fortune, not oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between culpable faults of judgment and outcomes determined by unforeseeable conditions; excessive self-reproach for unlucky results is misplaced.
